# Software stocks spared in tech rout as AI narrative shifts

Semiconductor and software shares now neck-and-neck in 2026 as investors think again about the technology’s winners and losers

![A trader sits at a desk surrounded by multiple monitors displaying financial data and news coverage on the New York Stock Exchange trading floor.](https://images.ft.com/v3/image/raw/ftcms%3Adee35e75-b4a0-4e1c-a3e7-6ea4f9cfa554?source=next-article&fit=scale-down&quality=highest&width=1440&dpr=1)

Emily Herbert in London

Published 28 minutes ago

Semiconductor and software stocks are neck-and-neck in market performance so far this year following a sharp turnaround in sentiment about the winners and losers of the AI boom, as a bruising tech sell-off upends this year’s popular trades. 

Software shares have been relatively unscathed by this month’s brutal rout in the tech sector, which has been concentrated in the semiconductor stocks that until recently were investor darlings. 

“The sentiment on semis is now exactly the sentiment we had on software six to nine months ago,” said Max Uleer, head of cross-asset strategy at Deutsche Bank. 

Investors dumped the stocks of software companies earlier this year on fears that advances in AI technology would undermine their business models. But the sector reversed those losses in the second half of the year and has held on to its gains in the recent volatility, highlighting a shift in how investors are thinking about the market impact of the AI revolution. 

“Undeniably, the narrative has moved for software as a sector, which was perceived as universally challenging, into a defined group of those who will be the structural winners and those who will not,” said Lawrence Jamieson, co-head of Emea equity capital markets at Barclays. 

![Line chart of Index change showing Software and semiconductors have converged for the year](https://images.ft.com/v3/image/raw/https%3A%2F%2Fd6c748xw2pzm8.cloudfront.net%2Fprod%2Fd45cd470-e8ee-11f1-81e8-2b891480dd1c-standard.png?source=next-article&fit=scale-down&quality=highest&width=700&dpr=1)

Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group, said: “The view from 40,000 feet is that markets don’t know who the winners and losers [from AI] will ultimately be.”

She said 2026 had been “a guessing game, where investors have made somewhat snap judgments, like the assumption that software firms and their products would become obsolete”.

“The thinking has evolved over time to questioning that thesis and ultimately worrying about semiconductors,” she added.

The software and semiconductor sub-indices of the S&P 500 are now both marginally negative year-to-date, with software stocks outperforming semiconductors.

The software sell-off at the start of 2026 gathered speed after the release of new tools by AI lab Anthropic, which gave users the ability to more easily perform complex legal, sales and marketing functions. 

As the sell-off deepened, being overweight semiconductor stocks compared to benchmarks while being underweight software stocks became a hedge fund favourite trade earlier this year. 

But the worst of the fears for the software sector have since faded, with investors reassured by the defensive value of companies’ large customer bases and their perceived “moats” of proprietary data sets. 

“Not all software businesses are created equal,” said Ben Preston, global equity strategist at Orbis Investments. “While some face genuine disruption, others possess proprietary data, embedded customer relationships and specialist expertise that AI cannot easily replicate.”

Preston said this year’s weakness in software stocks could create opportunities to “buy fundamentally strong businesses at attractive valuations”. 

The software rebound has been selective, with some names faring better than others.

Cybersecurity and data infrastructure companies have bounced back strongly, as the risk of AI-driven hacks and data breaches has become front of mind for policymakers and investors. CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks are up 72 per cent and 89 per cent respectively this year.

Big companies that were caught in the initial software sell-off — such as Microsoft — have rebounded, as investors come round to the idea that for those with large client bases and diversified revenues, AI can be an opportunity as well as a threat.

But others are struggling to win investors over. Salesforce and Adobe are down more than 30 per cent this year, and Intuit has lost 58 per cent. 

Marija Veitmane, head of equities strategy at State Street, said “the idea that we wouldn’t need software companies” was an “over-simplistic view of the world” and “clearly too extreme”. 

“The move this year is a normalisation of previous pessimism about software,” she said, adding that many of the big software companies “continue to show strong earnings and reliable sales”. 

Meanwhile, investors have appeared to sour on popular chip stocks, pushing the semiconductor sub-index of the S&P 500 into negative territory for 2026 despite a blistering rally at the start of the year. 

The force of the sell-off in chips has plunged the Nasdaq 100 index into so-called bear market territory in recent trading sessions, meaning it is more than 20 per cent below its recent peak.

This month’s US midterm elections delivered a heavy blow to the semiconductor sector, as the Democrats’ sweep of Congress and wins in key gubernatorial races stoked market fears of a policy and regulatory backlash to the pace of data centre build-out. 

Custodial data from State Street shows that institutional investors have sharply reduced their holdings of chip stocks in recent weeks and added to their software holdings at the same time.

However, some market participants said investors were still cautious about the software sector.

Jamieson at Barclays said initial public offerings, secondary share sales and other equity deals in the software sector were still subdued, making it hard to see evidence for an improvement in sentiment.

But Stan Hartman, head of Emea high-yield and leveraged loan syndicate at BNP Paribas, said the ability to do debt deals in the software sector had “improved” since the start of the year and that “you are seeing deals get done for existing issuers” — although investors were demanding more reassurance about the durability of companies’ revenues and their competitive moats.

However, he said investors were still “questioning businesses from call centres to software to business services . . . there continue to be a lot of questions about the evolution of these business models.”
